title: Blockchain Capstone Project
tagline: Plan, design, build, secure, deploy, document and defend one complete blockchain project
summary: The finishing course of the Blockchain & Web3 track. It guides you through one complete project from a real problem to a defended result: choosing and scoping with testable user stories and an honest comparison with a database, designing the architecture and a complete reference contract, building with tests first and randomised property tests, reviewing your own security with a threat model, deploying to a test network with verified source, writing documentation, and preparing a five-minute demonstration and a confident, honest defence. The reference contract compiles with solc against OpenZeppelin 5 and the JavaScript is syntax-checked. The platform does not run your project: you build and test it in your own tools on a test network, and nothing here is a security audit.

modules.title: Choose and scope your project
modules.summary: Picking a problem worth solving, writing user stories, deciding what is in and out, and an honest test of whether a blockchain belongs.
modules.outcome: You can pick a problem, write testable user stories, define a minimum viable scope and defend the choice of technology.
modules.intro: Most capstones are won or lost before a line of code is written. A well-chosen problem, a small scope and an honest answer to 'why a blockchain?' make the rest manageable. This module shows how to do that, with a concrete reference project that you can follow or adapt.

topics.title: Picking a problem worth solving
topics.html:
What makes a good capstone problem
QualityWhy it mattersExample
A real person has the problemYou can describe a user, not just a technologyA registrar who answers verification calls every week
It involves more than one partyShared records are where ledgers helpIssuer, holder and verifier
It can be finished in the time you haveA finished small project beats an unfinished large oneIssue, verify and revoke
It can be demonstrated in five minutesYou will present itA live verification of a real file
Risks are manageableYou can handle them responsiblyNo personal data, test network only
You can explain why not a databaseHonest reasoning earns trustA tamper-evident public record
Ideas that fit, and ideas to avoid
Fits wellAvoid
Credential or document verificationAnything holding real money for real strangers
Supply-chain status tracking among a few partiesAnything requiring unsolved problems such as secret national voting
A transparent donation tracker for a student fundA token sold as an investment
A ticketing or membership system with check-inA system that needs personal data on the chain
A registry of items with a trusted registrarAnything you cannot test thoroughly

Check what you just learned

1. Which is the best sign of a good capstone problem?
  • It uses the newest technology
  • It needs a token
  • A real person has the problem and it can be finished and demonstrated (correct)
  • It is very large

Problem first, technology second.

Check what you just learned

1. A capstone should be:
  • Untested
  • As large as possible
  • Secret
  • Finishable and demonstrable (correct)

Finished beats ambitious.
keyPoints: Choose a real problem with several parties, a finishable scope and a five-minute demo.
Avoid projects that hold real money or put personal data on a public chain.

topics.title: User stories and a minimum viable scope
topics.html:
Writing user stories that can be tested
PoorBetter
The system is secureAs a registrar, I want only authorised staff to issue so that strangers cannot create credentials. (Test: a stranger's call reverts.)
Users can verifyAs an employer, I want to drop a PDF on a page and see valid, revoked or does not match so that I can decide in seconds.
Fast and scalableAs a registrar, I want to issue up to 100 credentials in one transaction so that graduation season is manageable.

Defining the minimum viable project

  1. List every feature you can imagine.
  2. Mark those the demo cannot work without.
  3. Move everything else to 'later'.
  4. Write at least three things you will not do on purpose.
  5. Estimate the effort and compare it with the time you have.
  6. Cut until it fits with a buffer.

Check what you just learned

1. What makes a user story testable?
  • It states an observable result that a test can check (correct)
  • It is short
  • It uses technical words
  • It names a library

If you cannot test it, you cannot demonstrate it.

Check what you just learned

1. Features outside the MVP go to:
  • The trash with no record
  • A 'later' list (correct)
  • The demo
  • The contract

Keep them as future work.
keyPoints: Write testable stories and a minimum viable scope.
State what you will not do.

topics.title: Why a blockchain, and why not
topics.html:
An honest comparison for the reference project
QuestionDatabase run by the collegePublic ledger with a registry contract
Who must be trusted to keep records unchanged?The college, its staff and its servers, now and in the futureNo single party: past entries cannot be silently changed
Who can verify without asking permission?Anyone the college lets use its systemAnyone with an internet connection
What if the college closes or its website goes down?Verification stopsRecords and verification continue, provided someone runs a page
Cost and complexityLowHigher: keys, fees, a contract and monitoring
PrivacyEasier to protect and to correctPublic and permanent: only fingerprints may be stored
Speed to buildQuickSlower

A good capstone report says plainly that a database is a strong alternative and explains what the ledger adds in this case. A reviewer who sees that comparison trusts the rest of your work. A reviewer who sees 'because blockchain is secure' does not.

Check what you just learned

1. How should you answer 'why not a database?'
  • Databases are bad
  • Say it is more secure
  • Give the trade-off honestly and say what the ledger adds in your case (correct)
  • Avoid the question

Honesty is credible.

Watch out

Education only. A capstone on a test network is not a product, and real deployments need security review and legal advice.

Check what you just learned

1. A public ledger adds:
  • Faster building
  • Secrecy
  • Lower cost
  • A tamper-evident record independent of one operator (correct)

That is the case for it.

Key terms: flip and sort

Capstone
A final project that integrates what you have learned
User story
A short description of what a user wants and why
MVP
Minimum viable product
Scope
What the project will and will not do
Non-goal
Something deliberately left out
Stakeholder
Anyone affected by the project
keyPoints: Compare with a database honestly.
State what the ledger adds and what it costs.

modules.title: Architecture and contract design
modules.summary: From user stories to a design: components, data, roles, states and a complete reference contract.
modules.outcome: You can turn stories into a design, read a reference contract and estimate the effort honestly.
modules.intro: A good design makes the build straightforward and the review fast. This module walks from user stories to a component diagram, a data model, roles and a reference contract, and ends with a realistic estimate of the effort.

topics.title: From stories to components
topics.html:
Mapping stories to components
StoryComponentNotes
Issue a credentialContract function plus admin toolRole-protected; batch option
Verify a documentVerification page plus contract viewHash in the browser; read-only call
Revoke with a reasonContract function plus admin toolAllowed even when paused
Pause in an emergencyContract role plus runbookSeparate pauser account
Notice unusual activityEvent monitorAlert on Issued spikes and role changes
Keep personal data privateDesign ruleOnly fingerprints on-chain

Check what you just learned

1. Why is the verification step a read-only call?
  • It needs no wallet, costs no gas and anyone can do it (correct)
  • It is secret
  • It signs the document
  • It writes to the chain

Easy and free for verifiers.

Check what you just learned

1. A view call costs:
  • A lot
  • No gas (correct)
  • A token
  • A fee

Reads are free.
keyPoints: Map each story to a component.
Verification is a free read; issuing and revoking are role-protected writes.

topics.title: The reference contract
topics.html:
Design decisions to be able to explain
DecisionReason
Only a document hash is storedPublic, permanent chain: no personal data
ISSUER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE and the admin role are separateLeast privilege; the deployer holds no power
Revoke ignores the pauseCorrections must remain possible in an emergency
Revoke needs the original issuer or an adminOne issuer cannot cancel another's records
Batch size is limited to 100Avoids hitting the block gas limit
check returns an enumThe page can show a precise message
Custom errors and eventsCheap failures and monitoring
Expiry is optionalSome credentials do not expire

Check what you just learned

1. Why separate the pauser role from the admin?
  • It saves gas
  • Roles are required
  • A fast-response account can stop damage without power to change roles or issue (correct)
  • It hides the admin

Narrow, fast powers for emergencies.

Check what you just learned

1. The deployer after deployment should hold:
  • The keys of the issuers
  • All roles
  • Only the pause
  • No roles (correct)

Power goes to the admin and pauser.
keyPoints: Hash-only storage, separate roles, pausing that spares revocation, a batch limit and a clear check result.
Be ready to explain every design decision.

topics.title: Estimating and planning
topics.html:
Typical effort for the reference project (hours)
Task groupEstimateRisk factorAdjusted
Requirements and proposal81.2510
Contract design121.518
Implementation401.560
Testing and security review241.2530
Documentation, deployment and demo161.2520
Total100138

Does your plan fit?

Change your hours per week and weeks available to see whether the adjusted estimate fits. Cut scope if not.

Adjust Hours per week, Weeks until the deadline, Adjusted hours needed and see Hours available, Shortfall (hours), Weeks needed change.

Planning habits

  1. Plan in weekly milestones, each with something you can demonstrate.
  2. Do the riskiest parts first.
  3. Reserve the last two weeks for testing, documentation and rehearsal.
  4. Review progress each week against the plan.
  5. Cut scope early, not late.

Check what you just learned

1. Why add a risk factor to estimates?
  • Estimates are usually optimistic, and unknowns take longer than expected (correct)
  • To impress
  • Because tasks are easy
  • To reduce work

Plan for reality.

Check what you just learned

1. If the plan does not fit, you should:
  • Work all night
  • Cut scope (correct)
  • Skip tests
  • Hide it

Reduce the plan, not the quality.

Key terms: flip and sort

Component
A distinct part of the system
Role
A named permission
Least privilege
Giving only the power needed
Enum
A fixed set of named values
Estimate
A prediction of effort
Milestone
A checkpoint with something to show
keyPoints: Adjust estimates for risk and compare them with the time you have.
Do risky parts first and cut scope early.

steps: Draw the components and the data flow.

modules.title: Build the system
modules.summary: Tests first, a deployable script, a verification page, a repeat-safe workflow and weekly progress tracking.
modules.outcome: You can write tests that mirror requirements, create a rehearsable deployment, build a verification page and track progress honestly.
modules.intro: Building is easiest when the rules are already written as tests. This module shows a test suite for the reference contract, a deployment script and the verification page, and a simple way to track your progress each week without fooling yourself.

topics.title: Tests that mirror the requirements
topics.html:
Tests and the requirements they protect
TestRequirement
Issue and check ValidAuthorised issuers can record credentials; anyone can check
Changed document is a MismatchTampering is detected
Strangers are refusedOnly authorised issuers can issue
Duplicate ids are refusedA record cannot be overwritten
ExpiryCredentials can stop being valid after a date
Revoke with a reasonCorrections are possible and explained
Revoke while pausedEmergencies cannot block corrections
Batch limitA loop cannot exceed a safe size

Habits

  1. Write each test from a user story or requirement.
  2. Test failures as carefully as successes.
  3. Test the edges: zero, one, maximum and one over.
  4. Move time forward to test expiry.
  5. Run all tests before every commit.

Check what you just learned

1. Why test that revocation works while paused?
  • It is easy
  • Pausing is rare
  • A requirement says corrections must remain possible in an emergency (correct)
  • Tests must be long

Tests protect requirements.

Check what you just learned

1. Edge tests check:
  • Fees
  • Colours
  • Fonts
  • Zero, one, maximum and one over (correct)

Bugs hide at boundaries.
keyPoints: Write each test from a requirement and test failures and edges.
Move time forward to test expiry.

topics.title: Properties, deployment and the verification page
topics.html:
A property test states a rule that must always hold and then tries to break it with random sequences of actions. Here: once revoked, a credential never becomes valid again, whatever else happens. Reverts are fine. Breaking the rule is not.

What these three files protect
FileProtects against
Property testSurprising sequences that hand-written tests miss
Deploy scriptMistakes made by hand: wrong roles, wrong network, unverified source
Check scriptMisleading messages and wrong-network confusion on the public page

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the deployment script warn if the deployer still has the admin role?
  • Power should rest with the multi-signature admin, not the deployment account (correct)
  • Deployers are not allowed
  • It saves gas
  • It is a compile rule

Check the result of every deployment.

Check what you just learned

1. A property test checks:
  • One example
  • A rule that must always hold (correct)
  • Gas
  • Names

Randomised rules.
keyPoints: Property tests try to break always-true rules with random actions.
Scripts and clear messages remove human error.

topics.title: Working weekly and tracking honestly
topics.html:
Progress check

Enter the planned and actual hours to see how far along you are. A teaching tool.

Adjust Planned hours so far, Actual hours so far and see Progress against plan (%) change.

What to do when behind
SituationResponse
Slightly behind early onAdd a little time or trim a small feature
Behind with the riskiest part unfinishedCut features now; protect testing and documentation
Far behind close to the endPresent what works, state the limits honestly, and list the rest as future work

Common mistakes

  • Hiding delay from your supervisor until the last week.
  • Cutting tests to keep features.
  • Adding new features while behind.

Check what you just learned

1. What should you protect when time runs short?
  • The nicest features
  • The logo
  • Testing, documentation and the core journey (correct)
  • The newest library

Quality and honesty over breadth.

Check what you just learned

1. Being behind should be:
  • Blamed on others
  • Hidden
  • Ignored
  • Reported early (correct)

Early is cheaper.

Key terms: flip and sort

Test-first
Writing tests from requirements before or while building
Property test
A randomised test of an always-true rule
Deployment script
Repeatable code that performs a deployment
Milestone
A planned checkpoint
Burn-down
Tracking remaining work
Regression
A bug that returns after being fixed
keyPoints: Plan, build, test, demo, review and adjust every week.
When behind, cut features and protect tests and documentation.

modules.title: Security and quality review
modules.summary: A threat model, self-review, severity ratings, tools and the discipline of fixing what you find.
modules.outcome: You can write a threat model, review your own contract, rate findings and prepare for an external review.
modules.intro: A capstone that has been attacked by its author is stronger than one that has only been admired. This module teaches a structured self-review: model the threats, check the code against a list, rate what you find and fix or explain each item.

topics.title: Threat modelling your own project
topics.html:
Threat model for the reference project
ThreatMitigationRemaining risk
Stolen issuer key creates fake credentialsHardware wallets, role removal by admin, event monitoringA window between theft and detection
Fake verification websiteOfficial address published; contract and network shown on the pageUsers who do not check the address
Mistaken issue to the wrong personRevocation with reason, review before batchesShort period of misuse
Changed documentFingerprint mismatch is reportedNone for this check
Personal data leaking on-chainOnly fingerprints storedCertificate numbers linked to identities elsewhere
Admin key lossMulti-signature admin and a recovery procedureOperational mistakes

Check what you just learned

1. What is a residual risk?
  • A risk that remains after mitigation (correct)
  • A fixed bug
  • A type of fee
  • A role

Honesty about what is left.

Check what you just learned

1. A mitigation should be:
  • A hope
  • Specific and checkable (correct)
  • Secret
  • Long

Do something real.
keyPoints: List assets, actors and entry points, then ask what could go wrong.
Write the residual risks.

topics.title: Self-review, tools and severity
topics.html:
A self-review checklist for the registry
AreaQuestion
Access controlDoes every state-changing function have the right role? Is there a test from a stranger?
RolesWho holds each role after deployment? Does the deployer hold none?
PauseWhat does pausing stop and not stop? Is that intended?
InputsAre lengths, ids and reasons validated? Are loops bounded?
EventsDoes every state change emit an event that monitoring needs?
PrivacyIs anything personal written on-chain or in events?
UpgradesIs the contract meant to be immutable? Is that stated?
ToolsDoes static analysis show unexplained warnings? Do coverage gaps hide untested code?
A severity guide
SeverityMeaningAction
HighBreaks a core promise or can lose value or integrityFix before any launch
MediumA weakness with mitigations or limited impactFix or accept in writing
LowMinor or cosmeticNote and improve later

Using tools

  1. Run the compiler with warnings visible and read them.
  2. Run a static analyser and triage every finding.
  3. Check test coverage and look at untested branches.
  4. Use fuzz or property tests for rules that must always hold.
  5. Ask a classmate to try to break it for an hour.

Check what you just learned

1. Why ask someone else to try to break your project?
  • It is tradition
  • Tools cannot run
  • You are too close to your own work to see its weak points (correct)
  • Tests are optional

Fresh eyes find different problems.

Check what you just learned

1. A medium finding should be:
  • Deleted
  • Ignored
  • Hidden
  • Fixed or accepted in writing (correct)

A recorded decision.
keyPoints: Review access control, roles, pause, inputs, events, privacy and upgrades.
Rate findings and fix or accept them in writing.

topics.title: Preparing for an external review
topics.html:
What a reviewer needs from you

  1. A frozen version, tagged in the repository.
  2. A one-page specification and the threat model.
  3. Instructions to build and run the tests.
  4. A list of known issues and assumptions.
  5. Your own findings, rated and addressed.
  6. Time to fix and re-check afterwards.
How to respond to feedback
FeedbackGood response
A confirmed bugThank them, fix it, add a test and record it
A design disagreementExplain the reasoning and the trade-off; change if the argument is better
A request you cannot meet in timeState it as a known limit and future work
A misunderstandingImprove the documentation so the next reader does not make it

The attitude matters as much as the code. Reviewers respect students who welcome criticism, record decisions and do not defend mistakes. You are practising for a profession where this is the daily work.

Check what you just learned

1. How should you respond to a confirmed bug?
  • Thank them, fix it, add a test and record it (correct)
  • Argue
  • Ignore it
  • Delete the code

Learn and improve.

Watch out

A capstone review is not a professional audit. Real value needs independent experts.

Check what you just learned

1. Known issues should be:
  • Hidden
  • Listed honestly (correct)
  • Deleted
  • Blamed on tools

Trust grows from honesty.

Key terms: flip and sort

Threat model
A structured list of what could go wrong
Residual risk
A risk that remains after mitigation
Static analysis
Automated scanning for patterns
Coverage
How much code tests run
Severity
How serious an issue is
Audit
An independent professional review
keyPoints: Provide a frozen version, spec, threat model and known issues.
Welcome feedback and record decisions.

modules.title: Deploy and document
modules.summary: A rehearsed test-network deployment, verified source, a README, a user guide and an honest cost estimate.
modules.outcome: You can deploy to a test network repeatably, verify the source, write documentation that others can follow and estimate running costs.
modules.intro: Code that nobody can run or understand has little value. This module covers the last mile: deploying the same way every time, proving what is deployed, and writing the documents that make your work usable and credible.

topics.title: A rehearsed deployment
topics.html:
Deployment checklist
CheckWhy
Network name and chain id confirmed on screenAvoid deploying to the wrong network
Admin and pauser addresses typed twice and comparedA typo here is permanent
Deployer holds no roles afterwardsPower sits with the intended accounts
Source verified on the explorerAnyone can read what runs
Addresses saved to a file in the repositoryReproducibility
Demo run against the deployed contractProof that it works

Check what you just learned

1. Why type the admin address twice?
  • It is traditional
  • Wallets require it
  • A typo in a permanent role assignment cannot be undone (correct)
  • It lowers gas

Check what cannot be undone.

Check what you just learned

1. Verified source lets anyone:
  • Pause it
  • Withdraw funds
  • Change roles
  • Read what the contract does (correct)

Transparency.
keyPoints: Rehearse locally, deploy to a test network, verify source and save addresses.
Check roles and settings after deployment.

topics.title: Documentation people will read
topics.html:
The documents a reviewer expects
DocumentContents
READMEWhat it is, what it is not, how to run it, links, limits
User guideHow a registrar issues and revokes; how an employer verifies
Design documentArchitecture, data, roles, decisions with reasons
Threat modelAssets, threats, mitigations and residual risks
Test reportWhat is tested, coverage figure and how to run the tests
Deployment recordNetwork, addresses, roles, transaction links

Writing tips

  1. Write for a smart person who has never seen the project.
  2. Put the most important thing first.
  3. Use short sentences and plain words.
  4. Show screenshots or a short video.
  5. State limits in the first screen of the README.
  6. Test your instructions by asking someone to follow them.

Running cost

Change the costs to see the first-year cost per user. A teaching model in rupees.

Adjust Monthly running cost, One-off review, Active users and see First-year cost per user (rupees) change.

Check what you just learned

1. How do you know your instructions work?
  • Someone else can follow them successfully (correct)
  • You wrote them
  • They are long
  • They have screenshots

Test the documentation.

Check what you just learned

1. The first screen of the README should state:
  • Only a logo
  • What it is and its limits (correct)
  • Only a version
  • Only a licence

Honesty first.
keyPoints: Provide README, user guide, design, threat model, test report and deployment record.
Test your instructions on someone else.

topics.title: Operations and honest sustainability
topics.html:
If the project were real
AreaNeed
HostingA place for the verification page and the dashboard
RPC providerReliable chain access with a fallback
MonitoringAlerts for lag, errors and unusual events
Key managementHardware wallets and a multi-signature admin
SupportSomeone to answer users and handle disputes
Legal and privacyAdvice for the country and the data involved
Security reviewAn independent audit before real value or legal weight

A capstone does not need all of this, but your report should show you know what a real deployment would require. Estimating the costs and naming the responsibilities is part of professional maturity.

Common mistakes

  • Presenting a test-network demo as production-ready.
  • Forgetting that someone must pay for hosting and keys to be looked after.
  • Ignoring privacy law because it is 'only a student project'.

Check what you just learned

1. Why describe real-world operations in a capstone?
  • To make it longer
  • It is required by law
  • It shows you understand what a real deployment requires (correct)
  • It replaces testing

It shows professional maturity.

Check what you just learned

1. A student project still needs:
  • A press release
  • No documentation
  • No tests
  • Honest statements of limits (correct)

Integrity means stating limits plainly.

Key terms: flip and sort

Deployment record
A file with network, addresses and transaction links
Verified source
Source code matching the deployed bytecode
User guide
Instructions for people who use the system
README
The project's front page
RPC provider
A service giving access to a node
Runbook
Instructions for handling incidents
keyPoints: Name the operational needs of a real deployment.
State clearly that the capstone is not production-ready.

modules.title: Defence, presentation and career
modules.summary: A five-minute demo, answering hard questions honestly, and turning the capstone into a story for employers.
modules.outcome: You can present a clear demo, defend your decisions with integrity and describe your project and skills to employers.
modules.intro: The defence is where a capstone becomes a credential. Reviewers are not looking for perfection; they are looking for understanding, honesty and professional habits. This module prepares you to show them all three, and to carry the project into your career.

topics.title: The five-minute demo
topics.html:
Demo principles
PrinciplePractice
One storyFollow one user from problem to result
Show, do not describeLive actions on the test network
Break something on purposeChange a file and show the mismatch
Have a backupA recorded video and the links in a text file
Keep to timeRehearse twice with a timer
Finish with limitsState what it cannot do before they ask

Check what you just learned

1. Why prepare a backup recording?
  • Networks can be slow or fail at the worst moment (correct)
  • Live demos always work
  • It is required
  • It is shorter

Plan for failure.

Check what you just learned

1. A good demo shows:
  • Every feature
  • One clear story (correct)
  • Only slides
  • Only code

Clarity beats volume.
keyPoints: Follow one user story, show it live, break something on purpose and keep a backup.
State limits before the questions.

topics.title: Defending your decisions
topics.html:
Questions you should expect
QuestionWhat a strong answer includes
Why a blockchain and not a database?The trade-off, honestly, and what the ledger adds in your case
What is your biggest risk?A specific risk, your mitigation and what remains
How do you know it works?Your tests, including failure cases and a property test
What would you do with more time?A realistic list: audit, dashboard, privacy review
What did you get wrong?A real mistake and what you learned
How would this fail in the real world?Operational, legal and human failure modes

Habits of a strong defence

  1. Answer the question asked, briefly.
  2. Say 'I do not know' when you do not, and say how you would find out.
  3. Never claim your project is unhackable or perfectly secure.
  4. Admit mistakes and explain the fix.
  5. Know every line you present; do not show what you cannot explain.
  6. Thank the reviewers for hard questions.

Check what you just learned

1. What should you say when you do not know an answer?
  • Invent something
  • Change the subject
  • That you do not know and how you would find out (correct)
  • Say it does not matter

Honesty builds credibility.

Check what you just learned

1. Claims of 'unhackable' are:
  • Expected
  • Impressive
  • Required
  • A red flag (correct)

Overclaiming destroys trust.
keyPoints: Prepare for the standard questions and answer honestly.
Never claim perfect security.

topics.title: Telling the story to employers
topics.html:
Turning a capstone into career material
MaterialWhat to include
CV bulletBuilt and tested a credential registry on an Ethereum test network with role-based access, revocation and a hash-only privacy design; 15 tests including a randomised property test
Portfolio pageProblem, screenshot or video, architecture diagram, link to code and the threat model
Interview storyA decision you made and why, a mistake you fixed, and a risk you managed
Short pitchOne sentence on the problem, one on your solution, one on the honest limits

Next steps after the course

  1. Read audit reports of real projects and compare them with your threat model.
  2. Contribute a small fix to an open-source project.
  3. Try capture-the-flag exercises on contract security.
  4. Build a second project that uses a different pattern.
  5. Join local communities and ask for reviews.
  6. Keep your portfolio tidy and your claims honest.

Employers in this field have seen many projects that overclaim. The ones that stand out are small, finished, tested and honest. Your capstone is evidence that you can be trusted with more.

Check what you just learned

capstone.summary: Write the report of your complete project and pass the final assessment.
capstone.intro: This is the culmination of the track. Your capstone report is the document a reviewer reads before your defence: what you built and why, the requirements, the architecture and implementation, how you checked security and quality, how you deployed it, the results and your honest limits. Write it about the project you have built in your own tools; the reference registry is a fine choice. Then take the final assessment covering the whole course.
